evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Quercus macrocarpa and lists Texas in its native range.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list (Wildflower Center printable list compiled/managed by NPSOT Hill Country Chapter) includes Q. macrocarpa.
Bell County — Fort Cavazos identifies Bur oak as native to the installation.
Williamson County — a county archaeological/environmental survey describes historical bottomland forests containing Q. macrocarpa.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Purola Preserve separately lists its Q. macrocarpa occurrence as introduced at that site, so that local planted occurrence is not used as Hays native evidence.

morphology.look_here_first: Go straight to the leaf's deep middle sinuses and the acorn cup: bur oak often has a broad fiddle-shaped leaf with a narrow waist, and the huge cup wraps much of the nut with a conspicuously fringed or 'mossy' rim.
diagnostic_traits: large leaves often broadest toward tip with deep middle sinuses creating a waist
upper blade often shallowly lobed beyond the deep middle sinuses
cupule commonly encloses one-half or more of nut and bears long soft fringe around rim

confusers.separator: Chinkapin oak has chestnut-like regularly toothed leaves and a non-fringed bowl-like cup; bur oak has deep midleaf sinuses and the diagnostic mossy/fringed cup.
White oak has regular rounded lobes down the blade and a shallow non-fringed cup; bur oak's middle sinuses and oversized fringed cup are decisive.
Overcup oak has a cup that can nearly enclose the nut but lacks bur oak's characteristic long mossy fringe and differs in leaf form.

installation_guardrail: Do not install until Calvin explicitly approves B011 pass taxa.
